Victim selection considers transaction age, cost of rollback, and number of updates. Wait-Die is non-preemptive (older waits, younger dies); Wound-Wait is preemptive (older wounds younger, younger waits).

questions.text: Explain B+ Tree Indexing. Show how B+ tree insertion and node splitting algorithms operate. Construct a B+ tree of order $p = 4$ for inserting keys: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. Why is B+ tree preferred over B-tree for database index files?
questions.solutionOutline: B+ tree is a balanced search tree where all data pointers reside in leaf nodes, linked sequentially for range queries. Internal nodes store search keys as routers. Max keys per node = p-1. Insertion splits leaf when full, promoting median key to parent. Preferred because leaf link enables fast range scans and higher branching factor due to smaller internal node size.

questions.text: Explain Static Hashing and Dynamic Hashing. Discuss Extendible Hashing with bucket address table, global directory depth ($d$), and local bucket depth ($d_i$) during bucket splitting and directory doubling.
questions.solutionOutline: Static hashing uses fixed number of buckets causing overflow chains as database grows. Extendible hashing uses hash function yielding binary string; global depth d determines directory size 2^d. If bucket overflows and local depth di = d, directory doubles (d becomes d+1). If di < d, only bucket splits and local depth increments.

questions.text: Differentiate between Lossless Join Decomposition and Dependency Preserving Decomposition. Given relation schema $R(A, B, C, D)$ and FDs $A \to B, B \to C, C \to D, D \to A$, test if decomposition into $R_1(A, B), R_2(B, C), R_3(C, D)$ is lossless and dependency preserving.
questions.solutionOutline: Lossless join ensures natural join reconstructs original relation without spurious tuples (R1 intersect R2 -> R1 or R2). Dependency preservation ensures all FDs in F can be enforced by individual decomposed relations without computing joins. Use chase tableau: R1(A,B), R2(B,C), R3(C,D) has R1 intersect R2 = B, B+ = BCDA (superkey of R2, lossless). Check D -> A: not directly preserved without join.

questions.text: Explain Thomas' Write Rule and Timestamp-Based Concurrency Control protocol. How does it guarantee conflict serializability and freedom from deadlock?
questions.solutionOutline: Timestamp protocol assigns unique monotonic timestamp TS(Ti) to transactions and maintains W-timestamp(Q) and R-timestamp(Q). Write is rejected and Ti aborted if TS(Ti) < R-timestamp(Q). Thomas Write Rule modifies this: if TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), ignore the obsolete write instead of aborting Ti, allowing greater concurrency.

questions.text: What are Views in SQL? Explain the concept of Updatable Views and conditions under which a view cannot be updated. Explain View Materialization and View Maintenance strategies.
questions.solutionOutline: View is a virtual table defined by an SQL query. Updatable views must derive from a single base table without aggregate functions, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, or set operators. View materialization physically stores the view result on disk; view maintenance updates materialized views incrementally upon base relation modifications.

questions.text: Explain Shadow Paging recovery technique and compare it with Log-Based Recovery in terms of commit overhead, garbage collection, and checkpointing.
questions.solutionOutline: Shadow paging maintains two page tables: Current Page Table and Shadow Page Table. Writes are performed on new copies of disk blocks; at commit, current page table pointer replaces shadow page table pointer atomically. No UNDO/REDO log needed. Drawbacks: data fragmentation, large page table overhead, and complex garbage collection of unreferenced blocks.

questions.text: What are Heuristic Optimization techniques for relational algebra queries? Explain the push-down selection ($\sigma$) and projection ($\pi$) rules to minimize intermediate relation sizes with an annotated query tree.
questions.solutionOutline: Heuristic optimization transforms relational algebra query tree into an equivalent more efficient form using algebraic equivalence rules. Primary heuristics: push select operations down as far as possible (early reduction of cardinality), push project operations down (dropping unnecessary columns), and combine selections with Cartesian products into joins.

questions.text: Explain the Checkpoint mechanism in database crash recovery. How does the recovery manager use Fuzzy Checkpointing or Checkpointing with active transaction lists to minimize recovery time?
questions.solutionOutline: Checkpoint flushes modified buffer pages (dirty blocks) and log records to stable storage. During crash recovery, log analysis starts from checkpoint record rather than beginning of log. Active transaction list records all transactions running at checkpoint. Prevents redundant REDO operations for transactions already committed before the checkpoint.

questions.text: Explain Generalization, Specialization, and Aggregation in Extended Entity-Relationship (EER) modeling. Differentiate between Disjoint vs Overlapping and Total vs Partial specialization constraints.
questions.solutionOutline: Generalization is bottom-up abstraction synthesizing common attributes of lower-level entities into a higher-level superclass. Specialization is top-down differentiation into subclasses. Aggregation represents a relationship between relationships. Disjointness: entity belongs to at most one subclass (d) or multiple (o). Completeness: Total (double line, must belong to a subclass) or Partial (single line).

questions.text: What are Multivalued Dependencies (MVD) and Join Dependencies? Define Fourth Normal Form (4NF) and Fifth Normal Form (5NF / Project-Join Normal Form) with illustrative counterexamples of redundancy.
questions.solutionOutline: MVD alpha ->-> beta states that beta values are independent of other attributes for a given alpha. 4NF requires all non-trivial MVDs to have a superkey on the LHS. 5NF (PJNF) applies when a relation cannot be losslessly decomposed into smaller projections without losing information unless every join dependency is implied by candidate keys.

questions.text: Explain Granularity of Data Items and Multiple Granularity Locking (MGL) protocol. Describe intention lock modes (IS, IX, SIX) and provide the lock compatibility matrix in a hierarchical database lock tree.
questions.solutionOutline: Granularity defines the size of data items locked (database, area, file, page, record). MGL allows locking nodes at different tree levels. Intention locks signal locks held lower in hierarchy: IS (intention shared), IX (intention exclusive), SIX (shared + intention exclusive). Lock tree must be traversed root-to-leaf, releasing leaf-to-root.

questions.text: Explain Dense Index versus Sparse Index, and Clustered versus Non-Clustered Indexing. When is a sparse index preferred over a dense index on a primary key file?
questions.solutionOutline: Dense index contains an index record for every search-key value in file. Sparse index contains index records for only some search-key values (typically one per disk block). Sparse index requires file to be physically sorted by search key. Sparse is preferred for sorted primary files because it fits in main memory and drastically lowers disk I/O overhead.

questions.text: What is NoSQL Database? Compare Relational DBMS and NoSQL (Document, Key-Value, Columnar, Graph) database models with respect to schema flexibility, horizontal scalability, and ACID vs BASE consistency properties.
questions.solutionOutline: NoSQL provides schema-less, distributed, highly available data storage for unstructured/semi-structured big data. Key-Value (Redis), Document (MongoDB), Columnar (Cassandra), Graph (Neo4j). RDBMS guarantees ACID with vertical scaling; NoSQL follows BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) with horizontal scale-out.
